The administration said the minister merely implemented recommendations made by a joint committee established in 2016 under his predecessor, Mohammed Musa Bello, which reportedly found the university’s original allocation of 11,824.04 hectares excessive.
The protest, organised on Monday by the university’s Joint Action Committee (JAC), was against the reduction of the institution’s landholding to 4,685 hectares.
Reacting, the minister’s Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media, Lere Olayinka, challenged the protesting unions and other stakeholders to explain why the university needed more than 11,000 hectares after 38 years of existence.
He recalled that on November 10, 2016, the then FCT Minister inaugurated a 12-member joint committee comprising representatives of the FCTA and UNIABUJA to examine the university’s land allocation and other related issues.
The committee was also mandated to investigate encroachment by indigenous settlers, illegal developments on the Gwagwalada Mini Campus and the issuance of land titles for the institution’s two campuses.
Olayinka disclosed that five of the committee members were nominated from the university. They included Prof. Otaki Alanana, Prof. A. Mallam, Mohamed Kassim, A.E. Ripite and Sadiq O. Shuaibu.
He said the committee recommended that the university’s main campus, covering more than 11,000 hectares, was far beyond the land size recommended by the National Universities Commission (NUC).
According to him, the committee proposed 100 hectares for the institution in line with the NUC recommendation, and its report was approved by Bello.
Olayinka argued that rather than limiting the university to the 100 hectares recommended, Wike approved 4,519.80 hectares, bringing the total allocation to 4,685 hectares.
He said the approved land could accommodate more than 80,000 buildings if each plot measured 500 square metres.
The FCTA also accused the university of allocating portions of the disputed land to individuals and corporate organisations without obtaining the administration’s approval.
Olayinka specifically alleged that the institution allocated 100 hectares to the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) without recourse to the FCTA.
He questioned whether the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), Senior Staff Association of Nigerian Universities (SSANU), Non-Academic Staff Union of Educational and Associated Institutions (NASU), Students’ Union Government and the alumni association were unaware of the 2016 committee’s recommendations.
He said the involvement of five university representatives in the committee raised questions about the basis of the current opposition to the land reduction.
The minister’s aide further challenged the protesters to identify universities around the world occupying more than 11,000 hectares and explain the expansion needs that would justify such a vast landholding.
“Where in the civilised world is a university built on over 11,000 hectares of land, on which over 220,000 houses can be built at 500 square meters per plot?” he asked.
He also questioned how the reduction would affect the academic activities of students or the welfare of university workers.
“If the government that owns a university chooses to reduce the size of its land on which no structure has been built in the school’s 38 years of existence, what effect will that have on ASUU, SSANU and NASU?” he queried.
“Will that affect the payment of their salaries? Will it affect the students in terms of their studies?” he added.
Olayinka urged the unions to explain their opposition to the decision, insisting that the land was originally allocated to the university by the government.
“ASUU, SSANU and NASU should be honest enough to tell Nigerians what their real interests are in a land matter between a university and the government from which it got the land allocation in the first place,” he said.
The FCTA maintained that Wike’s action was consistent with an earlier administrative review, rather than a unilateral decision to take land away from the university.
